web_evidence.title: I Have Some Questions for You by Rebecca Makkai | Excerpt
web_evidence.note: A sustained opening excerpt shows Bodie narrating her own perceptions, dreams, travel, speech, and return to Granby as 'I'; she separately addresses Mr. Bloch as 'you.'

web_evidence.title: Every Story is a Second-Person Story
web_evidence.note: Makkai distinguishes literal second-person protagonist narration from the mode used in this novel: a narrator addressing much of the text to a named 'you' character. This confirms that Bloch is the narrative addressee, not a 'you' protagonist replacing Bodie.

web_evidence.title: A New Era for Boarding School Literature
web_evidence.note: Literary Hub explicitly identifies Bodie as Makkai's first-person narrator and discusses her narration of the Granby return and investigation.

web_evidence.title: I Have Some Questions for You Quotes
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly identifies protagonist Bodie Kane as the story's first-person narrator and attributes narrative passages to her.

web_evidence.title: “I Have Some Questions For You” Review
web_evidence.note: The review calls Bodie the narrator and explains that she recounts her return while directly interrogating someone from her past. Its phrase 'technically in second person' describes the pervasive addressee framing, not narration with Bodie as a 'you' protagonist.

person_note: The controlling narrator is Bodie Kane, who participates in both the present investigation and remembered school events and consistently narrates as 'I' or story-specific 'we.' Many quotes independently expose that voice, and the sustained excerpt plus explicit structural sources corroborate it. The novel frequently addresses Mr. Bloch as 'you,' prompting some reviewers to call the technique second person, but Makkai's own explanation distinguishes this named addressee from literal second-person protagonist narration. The address is therefore a feature of Bodie's first-person narration, not an alternating or controlling SECOND strand; no credible evidence indicates sustained base sections in another person.
